Élections : les jeunes et la politique,: Elections: Are Youth and Politics Two Irreconcilable Worlds?
« Je n’ai jamais voté et je ne sais même: “I’ve never voted and I don’t even know how it works.”
Abdellah Azzouz, intervenant au Forum Je: Abdellah Azzouz, community worker at the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel. Photo: Ramy Berkani
« L’une des clés de nos succès, c’est le: “One of the keys to our success is the youth vote, and we had trouble getting that vote out in Marie-Victorin.” Those were the words of Québec solidaire spokesperson Gabriel Nadeau-Dubois after his party’s defeat in the Marie-Victorin by-election last April. Five months later, and two weeks before the provincial general election scheduled for October 3 in Quebec, the subject of the youth vote is back. With each election, abstention among 18- to 25-year-olds grows. Why aren’t young people voting? Is it a question of age? Do they need to get into the habit of voting?
Ce phénomène est-il attribuable à un man: Is this phenomenon due to a lack of political education or to communication gaps? Do solutions exist? To try to answer these questions, La Converse looked into the distance between youth and politics.
« Je n’ai jamais voté et je ne sais même: “I’ve never voted and I don’t even know how it works.” “My vote is useless, because political parties don’t care about us.” “All we know is that (François) Legault is going to give us $500.” From Montréal’s South Shore to Laval, by way of Longueuil and the Saint-Michel neighbourhood, the answers from young Quebecers are much alike. “The political parties don’t come looking for us and our vote. They try harder to attract the seniors’ vote than ours, when we represent the future and the next generation,” says Rania, 21, who lives in Longueuil. Maxime Blanchard, a McGill doctoral student and co-author of a research report on abstention in the 2018 Quebec general election, talks about the notion of habit: “What can motivate young people to go vote is finding it ‘normal.’ They’re used to voting, so they’ll keep voting, and that habit will last their whole lives.”
Autre point – et peut-être le plus impor: Another point, and perhaps the most important one: young people don’t feel heard or represented. In other words, they feel that their concerns and their reality take a back seat for political parties. For many young people, that feeling creates a rift. “The main parties don’t talk enough about certain issues, including the ones that matter to young people, like the environment. That partly explains why young people feel less concerned by politics and voting.” That is the observation made by Nadjim Fréchet, a political science doctoral student at Université de Montréal, on abstention among young people. “They talk to us about housing, renovating public transit, building a bridge, but how does any of that concern us?” asks a Dawson College student who lives in Hochelaga.
« Certains d’entre nous vivent dans une: “Some of us live in great precarity as soon as high school ends. A precarity that pushes many to drop out of school, because they can no longer manage both,” he adds. On student and youth precarity, the Liberal Party announces measures in its platform. The party says it is committed to reviewing the Perspective Québec scholarship program announced by the CAQ government. The program helps young people pursue their studies. As for Québec solidaire, it proposes free education from primary school through university.
Ashley, 22 ans, vote, mais ne se sent pa: Ashley, 22, votes, but doesn’t feel represented by the parties all the same. “We should talk more about diversity. That’s what concerns us young people, and not only young immigrants. The reason we point to issues like systemic racism or the lack of representation is that it goes on and on. It’s a problem that should be dealt with more conviction and more depth.” A disinterest, even a disconnection, from politics, then, caused by politicians who are themselves disconnected from the realities and needs of Montréal youth.
<strong>Communication et éducation, les: Communication and education, the foundations of a good relationship
« Malheureusement, on ne nous a jamais p: “Unfortunately, politics was never introduced or explained to us; no one ever tried to make us like politics,” laments Rania, who lives in Longueuil. La Converse contacted Élections Québec and asked about this lack of political education among young people and the gaps in communication with them. “They can go directly to our website, or follow our advertising campaigns on social media,” the institution’s representatives replied. When asked what measures are in place in schools to spark young people’s interest in politics, they answered that “politics is taught in school from the youngest age.” A statement that reflects the problem of political education, which leads young people to drift away from the political sphere, and from the question of voting in particular. According to young Montrealers, Élections Québec and the political parties are disconnected above all in how they communicate. “Recently, they put out a video of themselves doing the Harlem Shake, a trend from 2013…” says Abdellah Azzouz, a young community worker in Saint-Michel, ironically. Asked about these problems of communication and political education, young Montrealers often use one word in their answers: “proximity.” “It’s election season, so of course you’re going to meet politicians and candidates, you’re going to see them come around pretending to care about the neighbourhood’s needs, but where were they these past years?” Azzouz asks again, with the same irony. These young people talk about proximity in human relationships, in meetings, in visits to the neighbourhoods and, above all, in listening. “Voting and getting involved in politics is something you learn. You don’t turn 18, reach voting age, and say to yourself: ‘Okay, I can vote.’ No, that’s not how it works,” says Mohamed Noredine Mimoun, coordinator of the Forum Jeunesse Saint-Michel. He adds that young people need to “receive an education well before they can vote, starting at 15 or 16.
À cet âge, tu commences déjà à comprendr: At that age, you’re already starting to understand how it works and why voting matters. When they reach voting age, it doesn’t speak to them, because they’ve learned nothing about it.” That is what our community worker denounces. It could also explain why not a single young person from the Saint-Michel neighbourhood showed up at the voting awareness event organized for them last Wednesday by the Forum Jeunesse Saint-Michel. “Politics isn’t these young people’s natural environment, but if we do nothing, they’ll keep on not feeling concerned by elections and voting,” concludes Mimoun.
Soucieux de corriger le manque d’éducati: Eager to fix young people’s lack of education and the poor communication from political bodies, Mimoun, who also works at CEGEP de Maisonneuve, praises Élections Québec for setting up polling stations in CEGEPs and universities: “Just knowing they can vote at their school creates a connection. Many young people voted for the first time thanks to this initiative, to this closeness of the vote.” For Said, 27, who lives in Saint-Michel, young people’s interests need to be represented and served. To that end, many initiatives are under way to bring youth issues to the attention of political parties. The organization Vivre Saint-Michel en Santé is holding a “public debate” on September 23. Community partners in the Saint-Michel neighbourhood are bringing together candidates in the Viau riding and residents to address the issues voted on by those same residents, including young people. The organization Un itinéraire pour tous (UIPT) is also working to help residents of Montréal-Nord get informed about the coming provincial election. How? Through the Engagement citoyen program, which aims to raise young people’s awareness of political and civic participation. “It’s important for them to get involved and make their voices heard. It’s important that they see themselves as holders of this power, the power to choose the people who will make decisions for them. They have to understand that,” insists Janvier Ndizeye, UIPT’s youth project coordinator.
Le programme compte plusieurs projets co: The program includes several projects, such as Moi maire(sse) de ma ville, a role-playing game in which young people put themselves in the place of elected officials to spark their interest. The group Les jeunes engagés, which represents young people, meets every Thursday and mobilizes other youth in the neighbourhood to fulfil this civic duty. That mobilization takes the form, for example, of video clips in which young people’s needs are laid out. During the video game nights UIPT organizes on Fridays or Saturdays, which draw many young people, one “jeune engagé” uses the opportunity to discuss the upcoming election, whether to explain the issues being debated or how the vote works. Ahead of this election, the organization is also presenting a series of six video clips that help people learn more about what the parties are proposing, while putting questions to them about neighbourhood issues: candidates in the Bourassa-Sauvé riding will, in fact, be questioned on education by young people from the neighbourhood. “We saw an improvement with the last municipal election, where young people who took part in our projects voted, when they had never done so before,” Janvier reports.
De retour à Saint-Michel, l’espoir est q: Back in Saint-Michel, there is hope all the same, despite the absence of young people at the political event organized by the Forum Jeunesse. That hope is embodied, notably, by Abdellah Azzouz, who is highly motivated to show the way to the young people of his neighbourhood. Like Les jeunes engagés, Abdellah, a community worker with the Forum Jeunesse Saint-Michel, is among those who still believe in rich relationships between youth and politics.
Malgré le désintérêt de plusieurs dans s: Despite the disinterest of many in his neighbourhood, young Abdellah, a Rosemont resident, has political ambitions to “change things,” he says. He is studying economics at Université de Montréal so that he can (as a first step) teach the subject at a CEGEP as a professor. But the young man’s ambitions don’t stop there… “I’m going to become premier,” he tells us. “You want to become a minister?” we ask. “No! I’m going to become premier,” he insists, with a smile that radiates unshakeable confidence.
« J’ai toujours voulu être premier minis: “I’ve always wanted to be premier, but I never talked about it, because people would have thought I was an idiot, but I know what I’m worth,” continues the aspiring politician, who doesn’t hesitate to share his views on his neighbourhood’s issues. He condemns the inaction of the federal, provincial and municipal governments on the question of gun violence. “Think about what you did wrong and what you failed to do for us to end up where we are today!” he had called out to politicians at a vigil last November.
Celui que l’on appelle simplement « Azzo: The man simply known as “Azzouz” in his neighbourhood arrived in Quebec in 2009. “My parents decided to come here because the health and education systems are much better for us and our future than in Algeria,” he says. By becoming premier, the young community worker hopes to be a source of motivation for others, but above all he would like to get involved to help people. “My mother and father can’t work with their degrees here in Quebec, like many people in that situation. Not every door is opened to them so they can integrate. Me, I want to open every door!” he concludes proudly.
Ouvrir des portes, voilà ce qui intéress: Opening doors: that is what interests this young man about politics. It is also with the aim of opening those doors that community organizations are mobilizing. Solutions and hope exist on both sides, but it is still too little to bring young people closer to politics or, at the very least, to their civic duty. A duty that, according to young people, should adapt to new generations and their ways of doing things, as with the arrival of electronic voting, for example.
